hints: Focus on what type of bond is actually being reduced in each case, a C=C double bond or a C=O carbonyl bond.
Remember that $\text{LiAlH}_4$ and $\text{NaBH}_4$ are hydride donors that attack polar $\text{C=O}$ bonds in aldehydes and ketones, not non-polar alkenes.
Check which starting materials contain a carbonyl group that can become an alcohol, and which one would need $\text{H}_2$ with a Ni or Pt catalyst instead.
walkthrough:
**Recall what hydride reagents do**

Think of $\text{LiAlH}_4$ and $\text{NaBH}_4$ as suppliers of $\text{H}^-$ ions. They love the slightly positive carbon in a polar $\text{C=O}$ bond.

General rule:
$$\text{aldehyde + [H]} \rightarrow \text{primary alcohol}$$
$$\text{ketone + [H]} \rightarrow \text{secondary alcohol}$$

**Test synthesis 1**

Starting material is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$, propene, which has a $\text{C=C}$ bond and no $\text{C=O}$ bond. Hydride reagents do not reduce isolated alkenes.

To make $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ you need electrophilic addition of hydrogen:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2 + \text{H}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Ni catalyst}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$$
So 1 is unsuccessful.

**Test synthesis 2**

Starting material is $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$, propanone, a ketone. $\text{NaBH}_4$ in aqueous or alcoholic solution reduces ketones cleanly to secondary alcohols.
$$\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3 + 2[\text{H}] \xrightarrow{\text{NaBH}_4} \text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$$
So 2 is successful.

**Test synthesis 3 and conclude**

Starting material is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, propanal, an aldehyde. $\text{NaBH}_4$ reduces aldehydes cleanly to primary alcohols.
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO} + 2[\text{H}] \xrightarrow{\text{NaBH}_4} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$
So 3 is successful. Only 2 and 3 work.

options.A: Incorrect. This would mean all three work, including 1. $\text{LiAlH}_4$ does not reduce a $\text{C=C}$ bond in propene, so propane cannot be formed this way.
options.B: Incorrect. This pairs 1 and 2. While 2 is correct (ketone to secondary alcohol), 1 is wrong because hydride reagents leave alkenes untouched.
options.C: Correct. Both 2 and 3 are classic carbonyl reductions: propanone to propan-2-ol and propanal to propan-1-ol with $\text{NaBH}_4$. Reaction 1 fails, so only 2 and 3 are successful.
options.D: Incorrect. This means only 1 works. In fact 1 is the one that fails, while 2 and 3 are the successful carbonyl reductions. Students choosing this have confused alkene hydrogenation with hydride reduction.
